title: GitHub - Yelar/noclip: A playable neural world model of the Backrooms
excerpt: A playable neural world model of the Backrooms. Contribute to Yelar/noclip development by creating an account on GitHub.
content_html:
Play, recorded from the screen. Click for the video with sound.

Updates on X: @yelaryss

A neural network that is the game. It is shown the last few frames and your keys and mouse, and it draws the next frame, ten times a second. There is no map and no engine behind the picture: rooms are invented as you walk.

It learned this from a procedural simulator of 18 Backrooms levels (in sim/), and is played without it. The model has 211M parameters, was trained from scratch, and runs in real time on one mid-range GPU.

The first frame the model invents for each of its 18 levels, from nothing but the level's number.

Try it

You need an NVIDIA GPU with about 4 GB of free memory, and Python 3.10 or newer (3.12 is what it was built and tested with, on Linux).

git clone https://github.com/Yelar/noclip
cd noclip
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m wm.play

On Windows the PyTorch that pip installs cannot use the GPU, so install the CUDA build first (with Python 3.12):

git clone https://github.com/Yelar/noclip
cd noclip
pip install torch==2.8.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m wm.play

Windows is not tested. It runs uncompiled there (compiling is used on Linux only), so frames take longer than the numbers below.

If it prints no CUDA device on a machine that has an NVIDIA GPU, the PyTorch that pip chose is built for a newer driver than yours. Install the build for your driver (pytorch.org); pip install torch==2.8.0 is what this was tested with, on a driver for CUDA 12.8.

The first start downloads the model (2.2 GB, from Hugging Face) and the autoencoder it builds on, compiles for about a minute, and then prints ready. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/.

If the GPU is in another machine, start it there and forward the port from yours:

ssh -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 you@gpu-machine

Controls: click the picture to capture the mouse. W A S D walk, Shift runs, F is the flashlight, N falls into a random level (noclip), the number keys or the level menu fall into a chosen one, R starts a new dream, E is meant to open doors, Esc frees the mouse. The settings panel changes the number of denoising steps and how often something is near. The record button saves the session as an mp4 in rec/.

Speed: a frame takes 47 ms on an RTX 5000 Ada (comparable to an RTX 4080) with the default 12 denoising steps, of the 100 ms the game gives it. On a slower GPU the game runs slower instead of skipping frames; fewer steps in the settings panel make frames cheaper, at the cost of dreams that fall apart sooner.

Without an NVIDIA GPU it starts on Apple's GPU or the CPU (--device mps or cpu), uncompiled and well below the game's speed: on 12 CPU cores a frame takes 2.5 s. The CPU path is tested; the Apple one is not.

What to expect

  • It holds together long enough for real play. A level stays a place for tens of seconds at a time. When the picture does dissolve, the server drops you into another level.
  • Walking and looking work. Doors and entities turned out to be harder. Both appear in the dreams, but not reliably when you ask for them.
  • Places are remembered for a moment. Turn around and the room is usually still there; walk away, come back, and it is not.
  • It looks like its simulator. 512x288 pixels, 10 frames a second, the simulator's textures and lighting.

How it works

  1. The simulator (sim/) is a batched ray caster written in PyTorch: 64 games at once on one GPU, about 300 frames a second with encoding. Each level has its own generator for the map, textures, lamps and entities. A scripted explorer plays them: it walks, looks around, opens doors, runs from what follows it, and dies.
  2. Frames to latents. A pretrained autoencoder (DC-AE, 32x downsampling) turns a 512x288 frame into a 16x9 grid of 32 numbers each. Two parts of it are replaced: the decoder is fine-tuned on the simulator's frames (34.8 to 37.1 dB on held-out frames, wm/ae_tune.py), and a small network is trained to give the encoder's latents several times faster (wm/enc.py).
  3. The model (wm/model.py) is a causal transformer over the latent grids of the last 24 frames. Attention is split into within-a-frame and across-frames-at-the-same-place. Each frame is told the action that led to it and the level. It is trained by flow matching: every frame of a window is predicted from the lightly noised frames before it, in one pass.
  4. Against drift. A model that has only continued perfect frames falls apart when it continues its own. So for half of the batches the context frames are the model's own one-pass estimates, and the targets stay the real frames (hat_p in wm/task.py). On a 71M model at equal training this brought dreams 5 dB closer to the simulator after 9 s.
  5. Memory of places (wm/memory.py). Besides its window the model is shown up to 8 frames from longer ago that were seen from nearly the same spot in nearly the same direction. In training they are picked by the simulator's recorded poses; in play the pose is reckoned from your keys and the frames are the model's own.
  6. Playing (wm/play.py, wm/fast.py, wm/web/). The context's attention keys and values are cached, so a denoising step costs one frame's tokens. Each frame is drawn in 12 steps with a second-order sampler, decoded, and sent as a JPEG over a websocket. The frame pass and the decoder run as CUDA graphs. Twelve steps are for stability, not sharpness: with 6 a single frame looks the same, but dreams fall apart sooner.

The released model
Parameters 211M (width 768, 16 layers, 12 heads)
Input 24 frames of 16x9x32 latents, 11 action columns, the level
Training data 16M frames (440 hours of scripted play) in the last stage; nothing but the simulator
Training from scratch, about 123M frames in stages while the simulator grew from 12 to 18 levels
Hardware 6 to 11 RTX 5000 Ada GPUs for two days
Replay of recorded keys, nobody steering its frames stay close to the simulator's for the first second (26.7 dB PSNR); twelve seconds in it draws rooms of its own (17.3 dB)

The three last action columns are not keys but the game's state: something is near, the lamps are out, the lamps are red. In play a director sets the first (the settings panel's "dread"). The model barely responds to it, and the other two are left at zero.

Train your own

Everything below needs one NVIDIA GPU. pip install torchvision lpips for the two autoencoder tools.

# 1. Data: 64 parallel games, 256 frames a chunk. A million frames are 61 chunks and about 9 GB.
python -m sim.gen --out data/train --name a --seed 1 --chunks 61 --ae dcae-lite
python -m sim.gen --out data/val   --name v --seed 2 --chunks 2  --ae dcae-lite
python -m wm.data stats data/train && cp data/train/stats.json data/val/

# 2. The model: size s is 71M parameters, b is 211M.
python -m wm.train --data data/train --val data/val --out runs/s1 --size s --frames 24 --mem 8 --hat_p 0.5 --steps 20000

# 3. Look at it, then play it.
python -m wm.sample --ckpt runs/s1/model.pt --data data/val --out runs/s1/dreams --ae dcae-lite
python -m wm.play   --ckpt runs/s1/model.pt --data data/val --ae dcae-lite

python -m sim.gen --preview DIR writes contact sheets and a video of every level, to see the simulator itself. With the released model's fast encoder, datasets render several times faster (about 300 frames a second): --ae dcae-lite,enc=PATH/encoder.safetensors (the file is in the model's folder, which python -m wm.play prints at start).

The released model was trained on several GPUs at once with a trainer that is not part of this repository (elastic.py in the code's comments; wm/task.py is its task, and wm/train.py runs the same task on one GPU).

tools/ has the measuring scripts: act_gain.py (which inputs the model responds to), blank_stats.py (how much there is to see in a dataset's frames), mem_gain.py (what the memory is worth), play_prof.py (where a played frame's time goes), sampler.py (how few steps draw the same frame), train_prof.py, sim_stats.py.

Dataset format

A dataset is a folder of chunks. One chunk holds B parallel episodes for T consecutive frames.

NAME-00000.act.npy   float32 [B, T, A]         action that led to frame t (act[t] turns frame t-1 into frame t)
NAME-00000.lvl.npy   int16   [B, T]            level the player is in (or is falling into) at frame t
NAME-00000.aux.npy   float32 [B, T, X]         ground truth for analysis: position, heading, nearest entity, ...
NAME-00000.lat.npy   float16 [B, T, C, h, w]   frames in the autoencoder's latent space; written last
meta.json            fps, resolution, names of the action, level and aux columns, the autoencoder
stats.json           per-channel mean and std of the latents, fixed for a model's life

Actions (A = 11), one row per frame: forward and right (-1, 0, 1), turn and pitch (the change during the frame, divided by its maximum), sprint, light (the flashlight is on), noclip (1 on the frame the player falls into the level lvl names), use (1 on the frame E is pressed), then the game's state: presence, blackout, red.

Licence and credits

Code and model weights: Apache License 2.0 (LICENSE).

The frame autoencoder is DC-AE-lite by MIT HAN Lab and NVIDIA (mit-han-lab/dc-ae-lite-f32c32-sana-1.1-diffusers), downloaded from its own repository at first start. The released decoder.safetensors is its decoder, modified by fine-tuning on this simulator's frames; encoder.safetensors is a separate network trained to reproduce its encoder's output.

  title={Deep Compression Autoencoder for Efficient High-Resolution Diffusion Models},
  author={Chen, Junyu and Cai, Han and Chen, Junsong and Xie, Enze and Yang, Shang and Tang, Haotian and Li, Muyang and Lu, Yao and Han, Song},
  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.10733},
  year={2024}
}

The Backrooms is a collaborative internet fiction. The level names and ideas come from its community wikis; the maps, textures and code here are this project's own. It is not affiliated with any Backrooms film, game or wiki.

content_html_zh:
Play, recorded from the screen. Click for the video with sound.

Updates on X: @yelaryss

A neural network that is the game. It is shown the last few frames and your keys and mouse, and it draws the next frame, ten times a second. There is no map and no engine behind the picture: rooms are invented as you walk.

It learned this from a procedural simulator of 18 Backrooms levels (in sim/), and is played without it. The model has 211M parameters, was trained from scratch, and runs in real time on one mid-range GPU.

The first frame the model invents for each of its 18 levels, from nothing but the level's number.

Try it

You need an NVIDIA GPU with about 4 GB of free memory, and Python 3.10 or newer (3.12 is what it was built and tested with, on Linux).

git clone https://github.com/Yelar/noclip
cd noclip
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m wm.play

On Windows the PyTorch that pip installs cannot use the GPU, so install the CUDA build first (with Python 3.12):

git clone https://github.com/Yelar/noclip
cd noclip
pip install torch==2.8.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m wm.play

Windows is not tested. It runs uncompiled there (compiling is used on Linux only), so frames take longer than the numbers below.

If it prints no CUDA device on a machine that has an NVIDIA GPU, the PyTorch that pip chose is built for a newer driver than yours. Install the build for your driver (pytorch.org); pip install torch==2.8.0 is what this was tested with, on a driver for CUDA 12.8.

The first start downloads the model (2.2 GB, from Hugging Face) and the autoencoder it builds on, compiles for about a minute, and then prints ready. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/.

If the GPU is in another machine, start it there and forward the port from yours:

ssh -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 you@gpu-machine

Controls: click the picture to capture the mouse. W A S D walk, Shift runs, F is the flashlight, N falls into a random level (noclip), the number keys or the level menu fall into a chosen one, R starts a new dream, E is meant to open doors, Esc frees the mouse. The settings panel changes the number of denoising steps and how often something is near. The record button saves the session as an mp4 in rec/.

Speed: a frame takes 47 ms on an RTX 5000 Ada (comparable to an RTX 4080) with the default 12 denoising steps, of the 100 ms the game gives it. On a slower GPU the game runs slower instead of skipping frames; fewer steps in the settings panel make frames cheaper, at the cost of dreams that fall apart sooner.

Without an NVIDIA GPU it starts on Apple's GPU or the CPU (--device mps or cpu), uncompiled and well below the game's speed: on 12 CPU cores a frame takes 2.5 s. The CPU path is tested; the Apple one is not.

会发生什么

  • It holds together long enough for real play. A level stays a place for tens of seconds at a time. When the picture does dissolve, the server drops you into another level.
  • Walking and looking work. Doors and entities turned out to be harder. Both appear in the dreams, but not reliably when you ask for them.
  • Places are remembered for a moment. Turn around and the room is usually still there; walk away, come back, and it is not.
  • It looks like its simulator. 512x288 pixels, 10 frames a second, the simulator's textures and lighting.

它是如何运作的

  1. The simulator (sim/) is a batched ray caster written in PyTorch: 64 games at once on one GPU, about 300 frames a second with encoding. Each level has its own generator for the map, textures, lamps and entities. A scripted explorer plays them: it walks, looks around, opens doors, runs from what follows it, and dies.
  2. Frames to latents. A pretrained autoencoder (DC-AE, 32x downsampling) turns a 512x288 frame into a 16x9 grid of 32 numbers each. Two parts of it are replaced: the decoder is fine-tuned on the simulator's frames (34.8 to 37.1 dB on held-out frames, wm/ae_tune.py), and a small network is trained to give the encoder's latents several times faster (wm/enc.py).
  3. The model (wm/model.py) is a causal transformer over the latent grids of the last 24 frames. Attention is split into within-a-frame and across-frames-at-the-same-place. Each frame is told the action that led to it and the level. It is trained by flow matching: every frame of a window is predicted from the lightly noised frames before it, in one pass.
  4. Against drift. A model that has only continued perfect frames falls apart when it continues its own. So for half of the batches the context frames are the model's own one-pass estimates, and the targets stay the real frames (hat_p in wm/task.py). On a 71M model at equal training this brought dreams 5 dB closer to the simulator after 9 s.
  5. Memory of places (wm/memory.py). Besides its window the model is shown up to 8 frames from longer ago that were seen from nearly the same spot in nearly the same direction. In training they are picked by the simulator's recorded poses; in play the pose is reckoned from your keys and the frames are the model's own.
  6. Playing (wm/play.py, wm/fast.py, wm/web/). The context's attention keys and values are cached, so a denoising step costs one frame's tokens. Each frame is drawn in 12 steps with a second-order sampler, decoded, and sent as a JPEG over a websocket. The frame pass and the decoder run as CUDA graphs. Twelve steps are for stability, not sharpness: with 6 a single frame looks the same, but dreams fall apart sooner.

The released model
参数 211M (width 768, 16 layers, 12 heads)
Input 24 frames of 16x9x32 latents, 11 action columns, the level
训练数据 16M frames (440 hours of scripted play) in the last stage; nothing but the simulator
训练 from scratch, about 123M frames in stages while the simulator grew from 12 to 18 levels
硬件 6 to 11 RTX 5000 Ada GPUs for two days
Replay of recorded keys, nobody steering its frames stay close to the simulator's for the first second (26.7 dB PSNR); twelve seconds in it draws rooms of its own (17.3 dB)

The three last action columns are not keys but the game's state: something is near, the lamps are out, the lamps are red. In play a director sets the first (the settings panel's "dread"). The model barely responds to it, and the other two are left at zero.

Train your own

Everything below needs one NVIDIA GPU. pip install torchvision lpips for the two autoencoder tools.

# 1. Data: 64 parallel games, 256 frames a chunk. A million frames are 61 chunks and about 9 GB.
python -m sim.gen --out data/train --name a --seed 1 --chunks 61 --ae dcae-lite
python -m sim.gen --out data/val   --name v --seed 2 --chunks 2  --ae dcae-lite
python -m wm.data stats data/train && cp data/train/stats.json data/val/

# 2. The model: size s is 71M parameters, b is 211M.
python -m wm.train --data data/train --val data/val --out runs/s1 --size s --frames 24 --mem 8 --hat_p 0.5 --steps 20000

# 3. Look at it, then play it.
python -m wm.sample --ckpt runs/s1/model.pt --data data/val --out runs/s1/dreams --ae dcae-lite
python -m wm.play   --ckpt runs/s1/model.pt --data data/val --ae dcae-lite

python -m sim.gen --preview DIR writes contact sheets and a video of every level, to see the simulator itself. With the released model's fast encoder, datasets render several times faster (about 300 frames a second): --ae dcae-lite,enc=PATH/encoder.safetensors (the file is in the model's folder, which python -m wm.play prints at start).

The released model was trained on several GPUs at once with a trainer that is not part of this repository (elastic.py in the code's comments; wm/task.py is its task, and wm/train.py runs the same task on one GPU).

tools/ has the measuring scripts: act_gain.py (which inputs the model responds to), blank_stats.py (how much there is to see in a dataset's frames), mem_gain.py (what the memory is worth), play_prof.py (where a played frame's time goes), sampler.py (how few steps draw the same frame), train_prof.py, sim_stats.py.

Dataset format

A dataset is a folder of chunks. One chunk holds B parallel episodes for T consecutive frames.

NAME-00000.act.npy   float32 [B, T, A]         action that led to frame t (act[t] turns frame t-1 into frame t)
NAME-00000.lvl.npy   int16   [B, T]            level the player is in (or is falling into) at frame t
NAME-00000.aux.npy   float32 [B, T, X]         ground truth for analysis: position, heading, nearest entity, ...
NAME-00000.lat.npy   float16 [B, T, C, h, w]   frames in the autoencoder's latent space; written last
meta.json            fps, resolution, names of the action, level and aux columns, the autoencoder
stats.json           per-channel mean and std of the latents, fixed for a model's life

Actions (A = 11), one row per frame: forward and right (-1, 0, 1), turn and pitch (the change during the frame, divided by its maximum), sprint, light (the flashlight is on), noclip (1 on the frame the player falls into the level lvl names), use (1 on the frame E is pressed), then the game's state: presence, blackout, red.

The frame autoencoder is DC-AE-lite by MIT HAN Lab and NVIDIA (mit-han-lab/dc-ae-lite-f32c32-sana-1.1-diffusers), downloaded from its own repository at first start. The released decoder.safetensors is its decoder, modified by fine-tuning on this simulator's frames; encoder.safetensors is a separate network trained to reproduce its encoder's output.
